title: Directions a Matrix Keeps
intro: A matrix moves every vector in the plane, and almost every vector ends up pointing somewhere new. This page asks the question that starts the whole subject: are there vectors that the matrix moves without turning? It builds the answer from the picture, writes it as $Av = \lambda v$, and finds such vectors by eye in the simplest matrices.

blocks.text: A matrix is a map of the plane

A 2×2 matrix is a rule that takes a vector $(x, y)$ and gives back another vector. Every vector is a combination of the two basic ones, $e_1 = (1, 0)$ and $e_2 = (0, 1)$, namely $(x, y) = x\,e_1 + y\,e_2$. A matrix is linear (it is a linear map, or linear transformation), which means it respects that combination: $A(x\,e_1 + y\,e_2) = x\,Ae_1 + y\,Ae_2$. So to know what the matrix does to everything, you only need to know where it sends $e_1$ and $e_2$. Those two images are the two columns of the matrix. Take

and then any vector follows: $A(x, y) = x(2, 1) + y(1, 2) = (2x + y,\ x + 2y)$. As a check, $A(1, 3) = (2 + 3,\ 1 + 6) = (5, 7)$. The unit square, with corners at $0$, $e_1$, $e_2$ and $(1, 1)$, becomes the parallelogram with corners at $0$, $(2, 1)$, $(1, 2)$ and $(3, 3)$. In the viewer below that is the shaded parallelogram with two grey arrows, and the dashed unit circle becomes the green ellipse.
Most vectors turn

Look at what happened to a few vectors. The vector $e_1 = (1, 0)$ points along the x-axis and $Ae_1 = (2, 1)$ points about 26.6° above it: it has turned. The vector $(1, 3)$ points at 71.6° and $A(1, 3) = (5, 7)$ points at 54.5°: it has turned the other way, by 17.1°, towards the diagonal. The vector $(1, 2)$ goes to $(4, 5)$, from 63.4° to 51.3°, a turn of 12.1° back. So a matrix generally does two things at once: it changes the length of a vector and it changes its direction.

That is the problem. A matrix with its turning mixed into its stretching is hard to understand and harder to repeat: apply it twice and both effects compound. The way out is to look for the vectors where the turning is absent, so that only the stretching is left. If there are enough of them, they give a different way of looking at the matrix in which it is simple.
The question, and its answer
Is there a non-zero vector $v$ such that $Av$ lies on the same line as $v$? Being on the same line means $Av$ is a multiple of $v$, so we ask for a number $\lambda$ (the Greek letter lambda) with

A vector $v$ that does this is an eigenvector of $A$, and the number $\lambda$ is the matching eigenvalue. The pair is sometimes called an eigenpair. The word is half German: eigen means own or characteristic, so these are the matrix's own vectors and numbers. (The quantum shelf meets the same idea in Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors (#/quantum/foundations/eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors), with complex matrices.)

Two details in that definition matter. First, $v \ne 0$. The zero vector satisfies $A\,0 = \lambda\,0$ for every number $\lambda$ whatever, so it would make every number an eigenvalue and tell us nothing. We exclude it by hand. The eigenvalue $\lambda = 0$, in contrast, is perfectly allowed: it just means $Av = 0$ for some non-zero $v$. Second, the eigenvector is only half of the story, because it comes with a number. The same $v$ cannot have two eigenvalues (if $Av = 2v$ and $Av = 3v$ then $2v = 3v$, so $v = 0$), but one eigenvalue can go with many vectors.
What the eigenvalue says
On the line of an eigenvector the matrix acts as plain multiplication by $\lambda$. So the size and sign of $\lambda$ tell you the whole story along that line.

items: $\lambda > 1$: vectors on that line are stretched, and they stay pointing the same way. For $\lambda = 3$ every vector becomes three times as long.
$0 < \lambda < 1$: vectors on that line shrink towards the origin, still pointing the same way. For $\lambda = 0.5$ every vector halves.
$\lambda = 1$: vectors on that line are not moved at all. They are fixed by the matrix.
$\lambda = 0$: vectors on that line are squashed to the origin. The matrix has lost that direction, and it cannot be undone. (A matrix with a zero eigenvalue has determinant 0 and no inverse.)

$\lambda < 0$: vectors on that line are flipped to point the opposite way, and also stretched or shrunk by $|\lambda|$. They are still on the same line, which is all that is required: $Av = -2v$ is a multiple of $v$.

blocks.text: Checking the matrix above

Try the vector $(1, 1)$ on $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$. Row by row: the first entry of $Av$ is $2 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 1 = 3$ and the second is $1 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 1 = 3$. So $A(1, 1) = (3, 3) = 3\,(1, 1)$. It is an eigenvector with $\lambda = 3$.

Try $(1, -1)$. The first entry is $2 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot (-1) = 1$ and the second is $1 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot (-1) = -1$. So $A(1, -1) = (1, -1)$, which is $1 \cdot (1, -1)$. It is an eigenvector with $\lambda = 1$: this matrix does not move that vector at all.

Now a vector that is not an eigenvector. Try $(1, 0)$: $A(1, 0) = (2, 1)$. Is $(2, 1)$ a multiple of $(1, 0)$? A multiple of $(1, 0)$ has second entry 0, and this has second entry 1, so no. Similarly $(1, 2)$ goes to $(4, 5)$, and if $(4, 5) = \lambda (1, 2)$ then $\lambda = 4$ from the first entry and $\lambda = 2.5$ from the second, which disagree. A single failing entry is enough to show that a vector is not an eigenvector.
Directions, not vectors

If $v$ is an eigenvector then so is every non-zero multiple $c\,v$, with the same $\lambda$, because $A(cv) = c\,Av = c\lambda v = \lambda (cv)$. For the matrix above, $A(5, 5) = (15, 15)$ and $A(-2, 2) = (-2, 2)$. Nothing changes by rescaling, so what is really being found is a line through the origin, a direction. People speak of 'the eigenvector $(1, 1)$' when they mean the whole line. The viewers print eigenvectors as unit vectors (length 1) to two decimals, so $(1, 1)$ appears as $(0.71, 0.71)$, which is $(1, 1)/\sqrt{2}$. The sign is arbitrary: $(-0.71, -0.71)$ would be just as good.
Seeing them in the sweep

Here is a way to find eigen-directions with no algebra at all. Turn a unit vector $v$ through half a turn, 0° to 180°, and at each angle split $Av$ into two parts: its part along $v$ (the dot product $v \cdot Av$) and its part sideways to $v$ (the cross product $v \times Av = v_x (Av)_y - v_y (Av)_x$, positive when $Av$ is anticlockwise of $v$). The sideways part is exactly the amount by which $Av$ has turned away from $v$'s line. Where it crosses zero, $Av$ lies on $v$'s line, and there the along part is the eigenvalue $\lambda$ (with its sign). The top right panel of the viewer draws both curves.

For our matrix this can be worked out. With $v = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$, $Av = (2\cos\theta + \sin\theta,\ \cos\theta + 2\sin\theta)$, so the along part is $2\cos^2\theta + 2\cos\theta\sin\theta + 2\sin^2\theta = 2 + \sin 2\theta$ and the sideways part is $\cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta = \cos 2\theta$. The sideways part is zero when $2\theta = 90°$ or $270°$, that is at $\theta = 45°$ and $135°$. There the along part is $2 + \sin 90° = 3$ and $2 + \sin 270° = 1$. The eigenvalues are 3 and 1 and the directions are 45° and 135°, the lines of $(1, 1)$ and $(1, -1)$, found without solving anything. At $\theta = 20°$ the along part is $2 + \sin 40° = 2.643$ and the sideways part is $\cos 40° = 0.766$, so $Av$ has length $\sqrt{2.643^2 + 0.766^2} = 2.752$ and is turned by $\arctan(0.766/2.643) = 16.2°$.

Eigenvectors you can see without algebra
Some matrices have a geometric meaning that gives the answer immediately.

items: A stretch, $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.5 \end{pmatrix}$, doubles x and halves y. A vector on the x-axis, $(1, 0)$, goes to $(2, 0)$: $\lambda = 2$. A vector on the y-axis, $(0, 1)$, goes to $(0, 0.5)$: $\lambda = 0.5$. A diagonal matrix always has the coordinate axes as its eigen-directions, with the diagonal entries as eigenvalues. Any other vector, such as $(1, 1) \to (2, 0.5)$, turns towards the x-axis.

A reflection across the line $y = x$, $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, swaps the two coordinates. A vector on the mirror line, such as $(1, 1)$, is not moved: $\lambda = 1$. A vector perpendicular to the mirror, such as $(1, -1)$, goes to $(-1, 1)$, its own negative: $\lambda = -1$. Every other vector turns, but nothing else keeps its line.

A projection onto the x-axis, $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, drops each vector straight down onto that axis. A vector on the axis stays: $\lambda = 1$. A vector on the y-axis is dropped to the origin: $\lambda = 0$. The matrix is singular, and the zero eigenvalue is how that shows. Projecting twice is the same as projecting once, and that is why the only possible eigenvalues of a projection are 0 and 1: if $Pv = \lambda v$ then $P^2 v = \lambda^2 v$, and $P^2 = P$ forces $\lambda^2 = \lambda$.

A rotation by 30° turns every non-zero vector by 30°. No vector stays on its own line, so there are no real eigenvectors. (There are complex ones, and they carry the whole story: see Complex Eigenvalues and Rotation (#/math/eigenvalues/complex-eigenvalues).)

A shear, $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, slides each point sideways by an amount equal to its height: $(x, y) \to (x + y, y)$. The x-axis, where $y = 0$, does not move: $\lambda = 1$. Every other vector is tilted. There is exactly one eigen-direction, and it is the first example of a matrix that is short of eigenvectors, taken up in Repeated Eigenvalues and Defective Matrices (#/math/eigenvalues/repeated-eigenvalues).

Where this goes next

Guessing eigenvectors by geometry works for the neat cases, but a general matrix needs a method. Finding Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors (#/math/eigenvalues/finding-eigenvalues) turns $Av = \lambda v$ into the characteristic polynomial, which has the eigenvalues as roots. Diagonalisation and Powers (#/math/eigenvalues/diagonalisation) shows what you gain from a full set of eigenvectors: the matrix becomes diagonal in their directions and its powers become easy. The sweep panel, the stretch and the other matrices are all collected in A Gallery of Matrices (#/math/eigenvalues/gallery).
Practice

blocks.title: Is it an eigenvector?
blocks.text: For $B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$, test whether $(1, -2)$ and $(2, 1)$ are eigenvectors, and whether $(1, 1)$ is.
solution: $B(1, -2) = (1 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot (-2),\ 2 \cdot 1 + (-2)(-2)) = (-3, 6) = -3\,(1, -2)$. Yes, with $\lambda = -3$: the matrix flips this direction and triples it.

$B(1, 1) = (3, 0)$. If this were $\lambda (1, 1)$ the two entries would be equal, but they are 3 and 0. Not an eigenvector. These match the viewer's preset a negative eigenvalue, whose readout lists $\lambda_1 = -3$ along $(-0.45, 0.89)$ (the line of $(1, -2)$) and $\lambda_2 = 2$ along $(0.89, 0.45)$ (the line of $(2, 1)$).

blocks.title: A multiple, and a negative multiple
blocks.text: $Av = 4v$ for some $v$. What is $A(-3v)$? Is $-3v$ an eigenvector, and with which eigenvalue?
solution: $A(-3v) = -3\,Av = -3 \cdot 4v = 4\,(-3v)$. So $-3v$ is an eigenvector with the same eigenvalue, 4. Scaling an eigenvector, even by a negative number, keeps it on the same line and keeps $\lambda$. Only the zero vector ($c = 0$) is excluded.

blocks.title: A projection with no picture
blocks.text: The matrix $P = \begin{pmatrix} 0.5 & 0.5 \\ 0.5 & 0.5 \end{pmatrix}$ projects onto the line $y = x$. Find two eigenvectors and their eigenvalues by checking vectors on the line and perpendicular to it.
solution: On the line: $P(1, 1) = (0.5 + 0.5,\ 0.5 + 0.5) = (1, 1)$, so $\lambda = 1$. Perpendicular to it: $P(1, -1) = (0.5 - 0.5,\ 0.5 - 0.5) = (0, 0)$, so $\lambda = 0$. Check that the matrix is a projection: $P(1, 0) = (0.5, 0.5)$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $(1, 0)$ onto the line, and $P$ applied again leaves it alone, since $P(0.5, 0.5) = (0.5, 0.5)$.

blocks.title: A vector that turns
blocks.text: For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ find $A(1, 2)$ and by how many degrees $(1, 2)$ turns.
solution: $A(1, 2) = (2 + 2,\ 1 + 4) = (4, 5)$. The angle of $(1, 2)$ is $\arctan 2 = 63.43°$ and the angle of $(4, 5)$ is $\arctan 1.25 = 51.34°$. The vector turns by $51.34° - 63.43° = -12.09°$, clockwise by about 12.1°, towards the eigen-direction at 45° (the stronger one, $\lambda = 3$). It is not an eigenvector, and the turn is the proof.
